cases.title: Topological Sort
cases.problem: You are developing a course selection recommendation feature for an academic administration system. Given a course dependency graph (adjacency list), where each course is represented as a string, please return a valid course sequence list such that all prerequisite courses appear before each course.
cases.strategy: Maintain an indegree table and a queue of zero indegree nodes; each time a node is popped, delete its outgoing edges.
learning_objectives: Understand how the indegree table records the remaining dependency count.
Master the strategy of using a queue to manage zero indegree nodes.
Be able to predict the state updates after popping a node at each step from a trace.

interaction_tasks.feedback_correct: Correct! You have mastered the indegree update rule.
interaction_tasks.feedback_wrong: Carefully check the current indegree table; popping a node only affects its immediate neighbors.
interaction_tasks.oracle: Determine whether the student's answer accurately includes the nodes among graph['B']'s neighbors whose indegree becomes 0.
interaction_tasks.prompt: The current head of the queue is node 'B'. Please predict which neighbors' indegree will become 0 and will be added to the queue after popping 'B'.
interaction_tasks.stage2_affordance: Click node 'B' and observe the animation of neighbors' indegree changes.

interaction_tasks.feedback_correct: That's right, this is the core invariant of Kahn's algorithm.
interaction_tasks.feedback_wrong: Please check the indegree table; what value do the nodes in the queue have in indegree?
interaction_tasks.oracle: Automatically check whether the answer includes 'the indegree of all nodes in the queue is 0'.
interaction_tasks.prompt: During the entire algorithm execution, what invariant property does the queue always satisfy? (Hint: focus on indegree)
interaction_tasks.stage2_affordance: Open the indegree table view and observe the correspondence between the queue and indegree frame by frame.

interaction_tasks.feedback_correct: Correct, a cyclic graph has no topological order; the queue will eventually become empty with remaining nodes.
interaction_tasks.feedback_wrong: Try to think: when there is a cycle, which nodes will never have a chance to get indegree 0?
interaction_tasks.oracle: Check whether the answer indicates that the algorithm eventually cannot process all nodes, or the queue becomes empty prematurely.
interaction_tasks.prompt: Add an edge D->A to the original graph to create a cycle. Describe how this will affect the algorithm's behavior.
interaction_tasks.stage2_affordance: Drag the mouse to add edge D->A in the graph, re-run the algorithm and observe the result.

interaction_tasks.feedback_correct: Explanation is very clear; you fully understand the state transition logic.
interaction_tasks.feedback_wrong: Please focus on 'C's immediate neighbors in the adjacency list, and check the changes in their indegree before and after.

interaction_tasks.stage2_affordance: Click on each step on the timeline to replay the synchronized updates of indegree and queue.

cases.title: Complete Knapsack Coin Change
cases.problem: A store cashier needs to give change for amount. There is an unlimited number of coins in the cash register, with denominations given by the array coins. Write a program to calculate the minimum number of coins needed to make up the amount. If it is impossible to make up the amount in any way, return -1.
cases.strategy: Update dp[c] in increasing capacity order, allowing the same coin to be reused.
learning_objectives: Understand that dp[capacity] represents the minimum number of coins to make up capacity.
Analyze how the coin loop and increasing capacity order allow coin reuse.
Be able to predict the next dp update based on the current dp state and coin denomination.

interaction_tasks.feedback_correct: Correct! You successfully applied the state transition equation.
interaction_tasks.feedback_wrong: Not quite. Please observe dp[capacity-coin]+1 and compare with the current value, taking the smaller one.
interaction_tasks.oracle: Check if the predicted value equals min(3, dp[3]+1)=3, correct if so.
interaction_tasks.prompt: Current coin denomination coin=2, capacity=5, before update dp[5]=3, dp[3]=2. Predict the value of dp[5] after update.
interaction_tasks.stage2_affordance: Click the dp cell to highlight the calculation process.

interaction_tasks.feedback_correct: Exactly! No coins are needed when the capacity is 0.
interaction_tasks.feedback_wrong: Think again: what capacity requires no coins to make up?
interaction_tasks.oracle: The answer must point out that dp[0] is always 0 and explain why.
interaction_tasks.prompt: In the complete knapsack coin change problem, regardless of how coins and amount change, which state's value remains constant?
interaction_tasks.stage2_affordance: Slide the capacity axis to observe the constant value of dp[0].

interaction_tasks.feedback_wrong: Removing a large denomination might require more small coins. You can try computing the new dp array.
interaction_tasks.oracle: The predicted answer should match the verifier's output for coins=[1,2], amount=11 (should be 6).
interaction_tasks.prompt: Original coins=[1,2,5], amount=11, minimum coins=3. If we remove denomination 5, leaving only [1,2], what will be the minimum number of coins?
interaction_tasks.stage2_affordance: Click the coin denomination label to add or remove denominations.

interaction_tasks.feedback_correct: Your explanation is spot on! dp[capacity-coin] represents the optimal state before using the current coin.
interaction_tasks.feedback_wrong: Note that dp[capacity-coin] holds the minimum coins to make up capacity-coin, adding the current coin creates a new plan.
interaction_tasks.oracle: The answer must explain that dp[5] is the minimum coins to make up 5, then adding one coin of 5 makes up 10, and compare with the current optimum.
interaction_tasks.prompt: Explain why when coin=5, capacity=10, the update of dp[10] uses min(dp[10], dp[5]+1).
interaction_tasks.stage2_affordance: Drag the coin to the corresponding capacity slot to see the combination process.

cases.title: House Robber
cases.problem: A thief plans to rob a number of houses along a street. The houses are arranged in a straight line, each containing a certain amount of cash, represented by an integer array nums, where nums[i] is the cash amount in the i-th house (0-based index). Since adjacent houses are equipped with connected alarms, robbing two adjacent houses will trigger the alarm. Help the thief calculate the maximum total amount of money that can be robbed without triggering the alarm.
cases.strategy: Use dp[i] to record the maximum profit from the first i houses.
learning_objectives: Understand that the state dp[i] represents the maximum profit from the first i houses and its recurrence relation
Predict the next step's calculation from the changes in the dp array in the trace
Identify and verify monotonic invariants in the algorithm (e.g., dp[i] >= dp[i-1])

interaction_tasks.feedback_correct: Correct! According to the transition equation, dp[2] takes the optimal value of either not robbing the current house (using dp[1]) or robbing the current house (dp[0]+9).
interaction_tasks.feedback_wrong: Recall the recurrence formula dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2]+nums[i]), and check the values of dp[0], dp[1], nums[2] again.
interaction_tasks.oracle: Check if the student's answer is max(dp[1], dp[0]+nums[2]) = max(7, 2+9)=11; can use verifier or direct calculation.
interaction_tasks.prompt: Given the house amounts nums = [2,7,9,3,1], the dp array has been completed up to dp[0]=2, dp[1]=7. When computing i=2, what should be the value of dp[2]?
interaction_tasks.stage2_affordance: Fill in the predicted value in the table and play the step demonstration.

interaction_tasks.feedback_correct: Great! The monotonicity of dp ensures that the optimal solution at each step does not degrade.
interaction_tasks.feedback_wrong: Hint: dp[i] represents the optimal solution for the first i houses. Could it be smaller than dp[i-1]? Think again.
interaction_tasks.oracle: Check if the student's answer includes dp[i] ≥ dp[i-1] or non-decreasing property, or not exceeding the prefix sum. Accept semantically equivalent expressions.
interaction_tasks.prompt: Observe the changes in the dp array throughout the algorithm execution and point out an invariant that always holds (e.g., what property does dp[i] satisfy?).
interaction_tasks.stage2_affordance: Switch to numerical comparison mode, highlighting changes in adjacent dp values.

interaction_tasks.feedback_correct: Correct! You successfully applied the algorithm to new data.
interaction_tasks.feedback_wrong: Hint: Consider whether to rob the 4th house (amount 1) or not, and compare with previous gains. Try running the algorithm manually.
interaction_tasks.oracle: Use verifier to compute expected = 4, judge whether the student's answer is 4.
interaction_tasks.prompt: If the house amounts are changed to nums = [1,2,3,1], manually calculate the maximum stealable amount.
interaction_tasks.stage2_affordance: Modify nums in the array editing area; the view and results will update automatically.

interaction_tasks.feedback_correct: Clear explanation! You accurately described the trade-off between robbing and not robbing.
interaction_tasks.feedback_wrong: Review the transition equation: dp[i] either inherits directly from the previous step (not robbing) or from i-2 steps plus the current house (robbing). Please describe again.
interaction_tasks.oracle: Check if the student states: dp[3] = max(dp[2], dp[1]+nums[3]) = max(11, 7+3)=11, with the decision being not to rob the 3rd house.
interaction_tasks.prompt: In the trace, when i=3, nums=[2,7,9,3], dp[2]=11 has been computed, and dp[3] is about to be calculated. Explain the decision process from state dp[2] to dp[3].
interaction_tasks.stage2_affordance: Click on this step to highlight the dp[i-1] and dp[i-2] cells.

cases.title: Binary Search
cases.problem: You work in a library where books with unique call numbers are arranged in order on shelves. Given a shelf array nums (each position i stores call number nums[i]), and a target call number needed by a reader, return the index of target, or -1 if it does not exist.
cases.strategy: Maintain a closed interval and discard half after comparing the midpoint each time.
cases.input_contract: Input: a sorted nums array and target.
learning_objectives: Master the update rules for left and right pointers in closed-interval binary search.
Be able to predict the next search interval based on the comparison between the current mid value and target.
Understand that the interval length strictly decreases while the invariant that target remains within the interval is maintained.

interaction_tasks.feedback_correct: Correct! left is updated to mid+1, discarding the left half.
interaction_tasks.feedback_wrong: Observe the comparison logic again: when nums[mid] < target, the search interval becomes [mid+1, right].
interaction_tasks.oracle: According to the code, when nums[mid] < target, left = mid + 1, right unchanged. So next step left=3, right=5. You can verify the next state in the trace.
interaction_tasks.prompt: Current search interval: left=0, right=5, mid=2, nums=[-1,0,3,5,9,12], target=9. nums[mid]=3 < target. How will left and right update in the next step?
interaction_tasks.stage2_affordance: In the visualization, click the next step button and observe the left pointer move to the mid+1 position.

interaction_tasks.feedback_correct: Exactly! This is the core invariant for the correctness of binary search.
interaction_tasks.feedback_wrong: Hint: If target exists, why can we safely narrow the range after each comparison?
interaction_tasks.oracle: The correct answer is B. Verification method: Initially the interval contains the whole array; if target exists, each update never discards the part containing target. Check the trace: at each step, left/right, the target index remains within that interval.
interaction_tasks.prompt: At any step of binary search, which statement about the search interval and target always holds? A. target is definitely in the interval B. If target is in the array, it is always in the current interval C. The interval length is always even D. left is always less than right. Choose and explain.
interaction_tasks.stage2_affordance: Highlight the interval and show the possible location range of target.

interaction_tasks.feedback_correct: Correct! Changing target to a value that exists reduces the number of search steps.
interaction_tasks.feedback_wrong: Think about when the algorithm terminates early? When mid exactly equals target.
interaction_tasks.oracle: Change target to a value that exists in the array, such as 5. Then the algorithm returns immediately when mid hits 5, reducing the number of loop iterations. Check: original target=4 does not exist, loop runs 3 times; after change, loop runs 1-2 times. expected should be the corresponding index.
interaction_tasks.prompt: Suppose nums=[1,3,5,7,9], target=4. Modify the target value so that the search can stop early (i.e., fewer loop iterations than the original search). Provide the new target value.
interaction_tasks.stage2_affordance: Provide an input box for the student to enter a new target and run the visualization.

interaction_tasks.feedback_correct: Good! This shows the limitation of basic binary search with duplicate elements.
interaction_tasks.feedback_wrong: Try constructing an array with duplicate elements where binary search might return a non-first occurrence position.
interaction_tasks.oracle: Counterexample: nums=[1,2,2,2,3], target=2, expected index of first 2 is 1. But basic binary search may return the index of a middle 2 (e.g., 2). Use verifier: expected should be 1, but algorithm output may be 2. The input constructed by the user should produce an incorrect result.
interaction_tasks.prompt: A student says: "As long as nums is sorted, binary search can correctly return the index of any target, regardless of duplicates." Construct a counterexample nums and target using an array with duplicate elements to show this statement is wrong (assuming the requirement is to return the first occurrence position of target).
interaction_tasks.stage2_affordance: Drag array elements to create duplicate values and observe the mid position changes.

cases.title: Unique Paths
cases.problem: In a smart warehouse with m rows and n columns, an inspection robot starts from the top-left charging point (0,0). Each move can only be one step right or down. Given the number of rows m and columns n, compute the total number of distinct paths for the robot to reach the bottom-right packaging station (m-1, n-1). Input variables m and n represent the grid's row count and column count, output an integer representing the total number of paths.
cases.strategy: The number of paths for each cell comes from above and from the left.
learning_objectives: Understand the state definition in a 2D DP table where dp[i][j] represents the number of paths from the start to (i,j).
Be able to predict, based on the current cell's i and j in the trace, how the dependent dp[i-1][j] and dp[i][j-1] combine to produce dp[i][j].
Master how to use the combination formula to verify DP results, and understand the correspondence between state transitions and movement rules.

interaction_tasks.feedback_correct: Correct! You understood the transition equation: the number of paths at the current position is the sum of above and left.
interaction_tasks.feedback_wrong: Please check the path counts of the cells above and to the left, and add them together.
interaction_tasks.oracle: Compare whether the student's input equals the value of the set at that step in the trace.
interaction_tasks.prompt: Currently computing dp[2][3]; above it dp[1][3]=3, to its left dp[2][2]=2. Predict what the value of dp[2][3] should be.
interaction_tasks.stage2_affordance: Click on cell (2,3) in the matrix view; it will highlight its dependencies (1,3) and (2,2).

interaction_tasks.feedback_correct: That's right, because the robot can only move in one direction (right or down), so the edge cells have only one path.
interaction_tasks.feedback_wrong: Review the robot's movement rules: it can only move right or down. Therefore, to reach any cell in the first row, the last step can only come from the left, and similarly for the first column.
interaction_tasks.oracle: Check whether the student's answer includes the idea that since movement is only right or down, edge cells have only one possible source (from the start).
interaction_tasks.prompt: Observe the DP table; the values of the first row dp[0][j] and first column dp[i][0] are always 1. Explain why they do not change.
interaction_tasks.stage2_affordance: Highlight the first row and first column, and display arrows from the start point, emphasizing uniqueness.

interaction_tasks.feedback_correct: Great, you've grasped how parameter changes affect the result.
interaction_tasks.feedback_wrong: Try recalculating using the combination formula C(m+n-2, m-1), where m=4, n=7.
interaction_tasks.oracle: Calculate the expected value using the combination formula C(new m + new n - 2, new m - 1), and compare with the student's input.
interaction_tasks.prompt: If the grid is changed from m=3, n=7 to m=4, n=7 (adding one more row), what will be the new total number of paths? Please reason based on combination numbers or the DP table.
interaction_tasks.stage2_affordance: Drag the slider to modify m or n; the DP table will recalculate in real time and display the new result.

interaction_tasks.feedback_correct: Yes, because the last step to reach (2,3) has only these two possibilities, so the path counts are added.
interaction_tasks.feedback_wrong: Think: to reach (2,3), where could the previous step be? Could it come diagonally?
interaction_tasks.oracle: Detect if the answer mentions both 'coming down from the cell above (1,3)' and 'moving right from the left cell (2,2)'.
interaction_tasks.prompt: Explain why dp[2][3] equals the sum of dp[1][3] and dp[2][2]. Use the robot's movement rules in your explanation.
interaction_tasks.stage2_affordance: Click on the dp[2][3] cell; arrows will appear showing the paths from above and from the left.

cases.title: Convex Hull
cases.problem: In express delivery, you are given a list of delivery points 'points', each represented by a 2D coordinate (x, y). You need to compute the vertices of the smallest convex polygon that encloses all delivery points, and return the coordinate list of these vertices in the output order of the Andrew monotone chain algorithm. The returned vertices should be arranged counterclockwise and not include collinear intermediate points.
cases.strategy: Sort the point set by coordinates, maintain upper and lower convex hulls separately, and use orientation/cross product to determine turns.
cases.input_contract: Input is a 2D array of points.
learning_objectives: Understand how Andrew's monotone chain achieves convex hull detection through alternating construction of upper and lower hulls.
Be able to predict the next operation based on the position of the current point in the trace and the lower/upper hull states.
Identify invariants during convex hull construction, such as turn judgment cross <= 0 indicating a need to backtrack.

interaction_tasks.feedback_correct: Correct! cross > 0 indicates a left turn, so convexity is maintained, add directly.
interaction_tasks.feedback_wrong: Please observe the sign of the cross value. cross > 0 means left turn, the current three points do not form a right turn, so no need to pop. Check the cross of the current lower[-2], lower[-1], current in the trace.
interaction_tasks.oracle: If the student answers add the point because cross((0,0),(1,0),(1,2)) > 0, it is correct; if answer pop, it is wrong.
interaction_tasks.prompt: When the scanline reaches point (1,2), the lower convex hull 'lower' is currently [(0,0), (1,0)]. Based on the cross calculation result, predict whether the next lower state will add this point or pop the last point and then add. Why?
interaction_tasks.stage2_affordance: In Stage2, you can drag the scanline to this point and observe the turn hint animation.

interaction_tasks.feedback_correct: Very good! Turn judgment is the core invariant of convex hull algorithm.
interaction_tasks.feedback_wrong: Recall that when three consecutive points form a right turn or are collinear, the middle point needs to be removed. The turn is determined by the cross value.
interaction_tasks.oracle: If the student points out that cross(lower[-2], lower[-1], current) > 0 maintains convexity, or that when cross <= 0, backtrack until the condition is met, it is correct.
interaction_tasks.prompt: During the construction of the lower convex hull, what condition ensures that each added point does not break convexity? Please describe using relevant variables from the state.
interaction_tasks.stage2_affordance: In Stage2, point pairs that do not meet the condition will be highlighted, and the cross calculation process will be shown.

interaction_tasks.feedback_correct: Correct prediction! This point becomes a new convex hull vertex.
interaction_tasks.feedback_wrong: Please re-run the algorithm or observe the geometric view. Point (1,3) is outside the current convex hull and will change the hull shape.
interaction_tasks.oracle: Recalculate the correct expected via the verifier and compare with the student's prediction.
interaction_tasks.prompt: If one point in 'points' changes from (1,1) to (1,3), how would the convex hull vertex list 'expected' change? Please try to modify and predict the new 'expected'.
interaction_tasks.stage2_affordance: In Stage2, you can directly drag a point and see the convex hull update in real time.

interaction_tasks.feedback_correct: Accurate explanation! This is the convex hull backtracking mechanism.
interaction_tasks.feedback_wrong: Check the cross calculation: the cross product of vector (1,0)->(2,1) and (2,1)->(2,0). If non-positive, a pop is needed. Please examine the turn animation in the geometric view.
interaction_tasks.oracle: If the student explains that because cross((1,0),(2,1),(2,0)) <= 0, so (2,1) is popped, and then rechecked until the condition is satisfied, it is correct.
interaction_tasks.prompt: From step 5 to step 6, the trace shows 'lower' changing from [(0,0),(1,0),(2,1)] to [(0,0),(2,1)]. Please explain why this step occurs and relate it to the cross value of the current point (2,0).
interaction_tasks.stage2_affordance: In Stage2, a slow-motion animation of this step is played, showing the popped point and the turn angle.

cases.title: Segment Tree Range Sum
cases.problem: The logistics center records the weight of parcels (in kilograms) every hour, stored in the array nums. Operators need to query the total weight of parcels from time point query[0] to query[1] (closed interval), then according to the received correction information update=[pos,value] change the weight at the pos-th hour to value, and then re-query the total weight of the same interval. Please use a segment tree to calculate and return the total weight before correction 'before' and after correction 'after'. The input includes the nums array, query interval, and update operation; the output is an object containing 'before' and 'after'.
cases.strategy: Segment tree node meta records the covered interval and interval sum; query sums along covering nodes; update path backtracks from leaf to maintain parent nodes.
cases.input_contract: Input nums array, query closed interval, and update single-point assignment.
cases.variant_name: Segment Tree Range Sum + Point Update
learning_objectives: Understand the representation of interval and sum in segment tree nodes (e.g., l, r, sum in meta)
Understand the backtracking update process from leaf node to root node during point update
Be able to determine the divide-and-conquer strategy for range sum based on node coverage

interaction_tasks.feedback_correct: Correct! Partial overlap requires decomposing to left and right child nodes for separate queries.
interaction_tasks.feedback_wrong: Note that the current node interval [0,1] and the query interval [1,3] only overlap in the right half, so both left and right child nodes need to be considered.
interaction_tasks.oracle: Check the order of child node calls triggered by this node in the trace. The answer should include seg_0_0 and seg_1_1 (or corresponding interval representations), fuzzy matching allowed.
interaction_tasks.prompt: When querying the range query=[1,3] on the segment tree, the current visited node seg_0_1 (covering [0,1], partial overlap), which two child nodes should be visited next?
interaction_tasks.stage2_affordance: Highlight the current node in the tree view, and click on child nodes to expand and view.

interaction_tasks.feedback_correct: Absolutely correct! The parent node's sum is always the sum of its children's sums.
interaction_tasks.feedback_wrong: Observe the node sum label, think about how the parent node's sum is calculated from its children.
interaction_tasks.oracle: The answer should be seg_0_3.sum = seg_0_1.sum + seg_2_3.sum, allowing variable names or specific values, as long as the equation is reflected.
interaction_tasks.prompt: After construction, the sum of node seg_0_3 is 12, its left child seg_0_1 sum=3, right child seg_2_3 sum=9, please write the equation that satisfies the relationship among the three.
interaction_tasks.stage2_affordance: Display the values on tree nodes, and allow students to click nodes to view child relationships.

interaction_tasks.feedback_correct: Correct! A new value of 9 will change the interval sum to 15.
interaction_tasks.feedback_wrong: The total before correction is 10. To change the total to 15, the difference is 5, so how much should nums[2] increase? Note the original value 4.
interaction_tasks.oracle: Calculation: before=10, update value at index2, after = before - 4 + new_val = 15 => new_val=9. Student answering 9 is correct.
interaction_tasks.prompt: In the original problem, update=[2,6] changes nums[2] from 4 to 6, and the corrected sum for interval [1,3] is 12. If you want the corrected interval sum to become 15, what should the value in update be changed to?
interaction_tasks.stage2_affordance: Provide a slider or input box to modify the value of update, and the array view and tree view will update the sum in real-time.

interaction_tasks.feedback_correct: Exactly! The sum of a length-1 interval is the element value at that position.
interaction_tasks.feedback_wrong: Recall the definition of a leaf node: when l == r, the node represents a single element, so what should its sum be?
interaction_tasks.oracle: The student should mention that the leaf node interval [3,3] contains only one element, so its sum is nums[3] (value 5), allowing keywords like 'leaf', 'single element', 'directly take value'.
interaction_tasks.prompt: When constructing the leaf node seg_3_3 of the segment tree, why does its sum equal nums[3]? Explain using specific values from the array.
interaction_tasks.stage2_affordance: Highlight nums[3] in the array view, and show its mapping to the leaf node seg_3_3 via a connection line.

cases.title: Two Sum
cases.problem: In an order fulfillment system, nums[i] represents the quantity of goods that can be directly picked from the i-th slot, and the order still lacks target units of the same goods. Find two different slots such that the sum of their quantities equals exactly target, and return their 0-based indices; if no such slots exist, return an empty array.
cases.strategy: Traverse the array, use a hash table to record the indices of values that have appeared, and check for the complement.
cases.input_contract: Input the nums array and target.
learning_objectives: Master the changing patterns of the seen mapping and the need complement value in one-pass hash table scan
Able to predict the algorithm's next operation based on the current scan position i and the seen hash table
Able to understand the efficiency improvement from hash table lookups through repeated experiments

interaction_tasks.feedback_correct: Correct! Continue to the next slot.
interaction_tasks.feedback_wrong: Please observe the current need value, and note whether that value exists in seen.
